summary: This RFC discusses how to treat several local networks at a site as one Internet network, hiding the internal connections from the outside. It looks at how to do address resolution for this arrangement and proposes approaches.

eli5.summary: Many rooms in one building share a single street address. This asks how to deliver mail to the right room without telling outsiders the details.

questions: how to treat multiple lans as one ip network
what is multi lan address resolution
how does an arp based bridge work
subtitle: Proposes extending ARP so several LANs can share one network number without telling hosts.

tldr.problem: A site with several local area networks should not give each one a distinct Internet network number, and should hide the internal connections from outside gateways and hosts.
tldr.mechanism: Special boxes attached to two or more LANs answer ARP queries on behalf of hosts on other LANs, relay searches for unknown hosts onto their other interfaces, and forward datagrams. Ordinary hosts keep using plain ARP.
tldr.outcome: The author argues for these 'transparent subnets' over the 'explicit subnets' of RFC 917, and asks the community to agree on a solution. The RFC proposes a protocol and asks for discussion.

facts.label: Suggested timers
facts.value: T1 under 1 minute, T2 ten minutes, T3 one hour

facts.label: Retries by a BOX
facts.value: Same as hosts, for example five

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 925 no recorded status and lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The text presents itself as a proposed protocol that asks for discussion and suggestions for improvements.

sections.title: The Multi-LAN Problem
sections.content:
RFC 925 was prompted by RFC 917, in which Mogul argues for explicit subnets inside a network. Here Postel argues for transparent subnets, supported by a multi-LAN extension of the Address Resolution Protocol (ARP, RFC 826).

The goal is to treat a set of local area networks (LANs) as one Internet network. Giving each LAN its own Internet network number is called inappropriate, and the internal interconnections should be hidden from people, gateways and hosts outside the site.

As a reminder of ARP, a host that wants the hardware address (HA) for an Internet address (IA) broadcasts a request, the host that owns the address replies, and the asker saves the answer in a cache.
sections.eli5: A school with many classrooms wants one street address, not a separate address for each room, and outsiders should not need to know the rooms exist.

sections.title: The Magic Box and Its Three Cases
sections.content:
The new element is a "magic box" (BOX), also called an ARP-based bridge. It is a computer attached to two or more LANs like an ordinary host. Hosts behave exactly as with basic ARP. The BOX keeps a cache of IA:HA mappings for each LAN interface, and entries time out.

When it hears an ARP query, the BOX checks its caches:

  • Case 1: the mapping is in the cache of the LAN the query came from. The BOX stays silent and lets the host answer.
  • Case 2: the mapping is in the cache of a different LAN. The BOX replies with its own HA on the asker's LAN, acting as the agent for the destination, and must then forward IP datagrams for that host.
  • Case 3: the mapping is in no cache. The BOX searches for it, then answers as in case 1 or 2.

The BOX also stores the sender's IA:HA mapping from every ARP request it receives.
sections.eli5: If the person asked about sits in the same room, the helper says nothing. If they sit in another room, the helper says 'give it to me and I will pass it on'. If the helper does not know, it asks around first.

sections.title: Searches, Timers and Loops
sections.content:
For case 3 the BOX keeps a search list of hosts it is looking for, with the sought IA, the interface the request arrived on, and the original requester's addresses. If the host is already listed, the search ends. Otherwise the BOX adds an entry and sends an ARP request on each of its interfaces. A reply goes into the cache and removes the list entry. If no reply arrives, the BOX does nothing and the entry stays on the list, since ARP has no negative answer. A BOX must retry as many times as ordinary hosts do, such as five.

The search list stops infinite relaying of requests. Its side effect is that a host that comes up later stays unreachable from other LANs until the entry times out. Three times are defined: T1, how long hosts keep trying ARP, T2, how long a search list entry stays, and T3, how long a cache entry stays. The rule is T1 < T2 < T3, with a suggestion of under one minute, ten minutes and one hour.

For regular datagrams, BOXes must decrement the IP Time-To-Live and update the header checksum, discarding the datagram at zero. This prevents transmission loops. The one suggested host change is to keep the mapping from the first ARP reply rather than replacing it with later ones.
sections.eli5: The helper keeps a list of people it is still hunting for, so it does not keep asking the same question forever. Each note on the list gets thrown away after a while.

sections.title: Problems and the Case for Transparent Subnets
sections.content:
The memo lists potential problems. Bad cache entries persist for T3, and could be replaced if BOXes treat a broadcast ARP reply as a command to overwrite entries. Hosts that do not implement ARP need another mapping method. LANs without broadcast need a static or dynamic table of all their hosts, and the BOX sends an ARP-type request to each of the other BOXes on that LAN. In the worst case each BOX table could hold every host in all the LANs, but they are caches, and the typical case is far smaller.

Broadcast is covered too. Address 36.255.255.255 (with an all-ones host number) means all LANs of that network, and a BOX must forward it, using a list of recent broadcasts (source IA and Identification field) to avoid loops. Address 255.255.255.255 means this LAN only and is not forwarded.

In the comparison with explicit subnets, transparent subnets need no subnet field in the address, work with any address class including class C, and let a host move to another LAN without changing its IA. Hosts always just use ARP, and BOXes need no BOX-to-BOX protocol or topology knowledge. Trees of LANs need no search lists; loops need them. For very complex or unbalanced topologies, a BOX-to-BOX routing protocol may be better.
sections.eli5: The author says it is better if kids never need to know how the building is arranged. The helpers work it out quietly, and a child can move to a new room and keep the same name.

sections.title: The Recommendation
sections.content:
The author asks the Internet community to agree on a solution to the multi-LAN problem and to urge workstation manufacturers to build it in. He urges consideration of the extended ARP scheme, expects most workstations to sit on LANs with broadcast, and thinks most will not need explicit subnets and will fit class C addresses.

Neither this note nor RFC 917 proposes a specific routing procedure or BOX-to-BOX protocol, because routing between boxes is a very hard problem. If one is chosen later, the BOXes can be redone without redoing the hosts.
sections.eli5: He says: let us all pick one simple plan, ask the makers of computers to build it in, and fix the fancy parts later without touching the computers.

viz.caption: HOW THE BOX HANDLES AN ARP QUERY (RFC 925)

items.title: Case 1: same LAN
items.text: Mapping found in the cache of the asker's LAN. The BOX does not respond.

items.title: Case 2: other LAN
items.text: Mapping found in another LAN's cache. The BOX replies with its own HA and acts as agent.

items.title: Case 3: unknown
items.text: Not in any cache. The BOX searches on its interfaces, then answers as in case 1 or 2.

cells: Routing table kept up to date, probably by a BOX-to-BOX protocol
